title: The Hidden Trade Beneath the Forest Floor

passage.title: The Hidden Trade Beneath the Forest Floor
passage.author: BEACON Assessment Lab
passage.text:
When hikers walk through a quiet pine wood, the tall trees above them seem to stand alone. Each trunk rises toward the sun as if competing against its neighbors for light and space. Beneath the dark leaf litter, though, a dense web of tiny threads grows. It links almost every root tip in the soil. Scientists call this underground system a mycorrhizal web. Far from standing alone, forest trees use this living web to share food, water, and warning signals across long distances.

This partnership works because trees and fungi have very different strengths. Green needles high in the crown soak up sun and turn carbon gas into sweet liquid sugar. Yet thick tree roots cannot squeeze into tiny stone cracks. Fungal threads cannot make their own food from sun, but they excel at mining nitrogen and zinc from deep clay. Dissolved soil minerals, gathered from narrow rock pores by silky fungal threads, are steadily traded to towering fir trees in exchange for liquid sugar. Both partners thrive through this steady underground barter.

Field studies show that the fungal web also acts as a lifeline for young saplings growing in deep shade. Because thick branches block the sun, a small seedling on the forest floor often struggles to make enough sugar to survive. Older hub trees, which scientists sometimes call mother trees, pump extra carbon through the fungal conduit directly into the roots of shaded seedlings. In one forest test, a team traced carbon moving from tall birch trees. The carbon flowed into young firs when summer shade was deepest. Once autumn arrived and the birch leaves fell, the young firs sent small amounts of sugar back to the bare birch roots.

Beyond sharing food, the root web serves as an early warning system against insect pests. When bark beetles chew on the needles of a single pine, the hurt tree sends chemical signals into its root tips. Within hours, those signals travel through the fungal threads to healthy pines yards away. Upon receiving the warning, the untouched pines begin brewing bitter resins in their bark before the beetles even arrive.

These new findings have changed how foresters care for woods. In the past, loggers often cleared every old tree from a hillside and left young seedlings to grow in bare soil. Today, forest crews know that keeping older hub trees intact saves the vital fungal web below the ground. Guarding the unseen threads beneath the dirt is just as key as saving the tall timber above.

monsterSentence.verbatimSentence: Dissolved soil minerals, gathered from narrow rock pores by silky fungal threads, are steadily traded to towering fir trees in exchange for liquid sugar.
distractorChunks: to towering fir trees in exchange for liquid sugar
monsterSentence.activeRewrite: Silky fungal threads gather dissolved soil minerals from narrow rock pores and steadily trade them to towering fir trees in exchange for liquid sugar.

tier2Words.definition: To trade goods or services directly without using money
tier2Words.contextClue: Soil minerals 'are steadily traded to towering fir trees in exchange for liquid sugar.'

tier2Words.definition: A channel, pipe, or pathway through which fluids or signals travel
tier2Words.rootHint: con- + duct (Latin root meaning 'to lead together')
tier2Words.contextClue: Mother trees 'pump extra carbon through the fungal conduit directly into the roots of shaded seedlings.'

tier2Words.definition: Whole, undamaged, and left in its complete state
tier2Words.contextClue: Contrasted with 'cleared every old tree from a hillside' in the previous sentence.

tier2Words.definition: Essential or necessary for life and survival
tier2Words.contextClue: The network acts as a 'lifeline for young saplings' and protects the whole woodland.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 2:

"Dissolved soil minerals, gathered from narrow rock pores by silky fungal threads, are steadily traded to towering fir trees in exchange for liquid sugar."

In this sentence, what is being traded to the towering fir trees?

options.text: Narrow rock pores located deep inside the clay
options.diagnosticNote: Picks the object of the preposition 'from narrow rock pores' inside the middle modifier instead of the grammatical subject.
options.childFeedback: Narrow rock pores are the tiny spaces inside the clay where the minerals were hiding, not the items traded to the trees.

options.text: Silky fungal threads that grow into tall tree trunks
options.diagnosticNote: Confuses the agent collecting the minerals ('by silky fungal threads') with the item traded to the trees.
options.childFeedback: Silky fungal threads are the underground partners that gather the minerals, and fungal threads never grow into tall tree trunks.

options.text: Liquid sugar made from sunlight in the green canopy
options.diagnosticNote: Reverses the trade: the fir trees give liquid sugar to the fungi, while receiving dissolved soil minerals.
options.childFeedback: Liquid sugar is what the towering fir trees give back ('in exchange for liquid sugar'), whereas dissolved soil minerals are what get traded TO the fir trees.

options.text: Dissolved soil minerals collected by the fungi
options.diagnosticNote: Correctly links the grammatical subject 'Dissolved soil minerals' across the 9-word participial clause to the verb 'are steadily traded'.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 2, the subject 'Dissolved soil minerals... are steadily traded to towering fir trees' tells us that dissolved soil minerals collected by the fungi are what the fir trees receive.

questions.provingSentenceText: Dissolved soil minerals, gathered from narrow rock pores by silky fungal threads, are steadily traded to towering fir trees in exchange for liquid sugar.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 2, the subject 'Dissolved soil minerals... are steadily traded to towering fir trees' tells us that dissolved soil minerals collected by the fungi are what the fir trees receive.
questions.parentExplanation: This Sentence Surgery question tests Nested Clauses & Passive Tracking (ELAGSE5L1). When students strip out the embedded modifier ', gathered from narrow rock pores by silky fungal threads,', the core clause reads: 'Dissolved soil minerals... are steadily traded to towering fir trees.'
questions.retryHint: Find the main subject right before the comma and matching verb 'are steadily traded to towering fir trees' in Paragraph 2.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 3:

"Older hub trees, which scientists sometimes call mother trees, pump extra carbon through the fungal conduit directly into the roots of shaded seedlings."

What does the word conduit most likely mean as it is used in the sentence?

options.text: A connecting pathway or channel
options.diagnosticNote: Uses the root 'duct' (to lead) and context clues ('pump extra carbon through... directly into the roots') to identify a pathway.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 3, 'conduit' means a connecting pathway or channel, because older hub trees pump extra carbon through the fungal threads directly into the roots of shaded seedlings.

options.text: A poisonous chemical that blocks root growth
options.diagnosticNote: Contradicts the sentence context, where extra carbon is pumped through the conduit to help shaded seedlings survive.
options.childFeedback: Instead of blocking growth with poison, the fungal conduit delivers life-saving carbon to help shaded seedlings survive.

options.text: A dense shadow cast by tall branches
options.diagnosticNote: Borrows the nearby concept of 'shaded seedlings' rather than decoding the noun through which carbon is pumped.
options.childFeedback: The dense shadow in Paragraph 3 is caused by thick branches overhead, whereas the fungal conduit is underground connecting the tree roots.

options.text: A metal tool used by forest researchers
options.diagnosticNote: Assumes 'conduit' refers to human laboratory equipment rather than the natural 'fungal conduit' described.
options.childFeedback: The fungal conduit is a natural living pathway made of fungal threads in the soil, not a metal tool carried by human researchers.

questions.provingSentenceText: Older hub trees, which scientists sometimes call mother trees, pump extra carbon through the fungal conduit directly into the roots of shaded seedlings.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 3, 'conduit' means a connecting pathway or channel, because older hub trees pump extra carbon through the fungal threads directly into the roots of shaded seedlings.
questions.parentExplanation: Contextual vocabulary item (ELAGSE5RI4). The preposition 'through' paired with the verb 'pump... directly into the roots' signals that a 'fungal conduit' is a connecting tube, channel, or pathway.
questions.retryHint: Picture how carbon travels 'through the fungal conduit directly into the roots' in Paragraph 3, like water flowing through a pipe or channel.

questions.prompt: Based on Paragraph 4, how does the mycorrhizal network help untouched pine trees survive a bark beetle outbreak?

options.text: The fungal threads wrap around the beetles on the bark and trap them before they can fly.
options.diagnosticNote: Invents an unsupported physical attack by underground fungi on tree-dwelling beetles.
options.childFeedback: Fungal threads grow underground beneath the leaf litter (Paragraph 1); they do not climb tree bark to trap flying beetles.

options.text: Injured pine trees drain all the water from nearby trees so the beetles have nothing left to eat.
options.diagnosticNote: Reverses the cooperative relationship described in Paragraph 4 into a harmful one.
options.childFeedback: Injured pines do not drain water from their neighbors; instead, they send helpful chemical warning signals through the root web.

options.text: Chemical warning signals travel through the root web so neighboring pines can produce bitter resins before the insects arrive.
options.diagnosticNote: Accurately traces the cause-and-effect chain in Paragraph 4 from root distress signals to defensive bitter resins.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 4 explains that when bark beetles bite one pine tree, chemical warning signals travel through the fungal root web so neighboring pines can brew bitter resins before the beetles arrive.

options.text: The network guarantees that no insect can ever bite a single pine needle in the forest.
options.diagnosticNote: Uses extreme language ('guarantees', 'no insect can ever') that contradicts the first pine being chewed by beetles.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 4 starts with bark beetles chewing on the needles of a pine tree, so the network does not stop every single bite—it helps neighboring trees prepare defenses.

questions.provingSentenceText: Upon receiving the warning, the untouched pines begin brewing bitter resins in their bark before the beetles even arrive.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 4 explains that when bark beetles bite one pine tree, chemical warning signals travel through the fungal root web so neighboring pines can brew bitter resins before the beetles arrive.
questions.parentExplanation: This Click-to-Prove item tests scientific cause-and-effect relationships (ELAGSE5RI3). Paragraph 4 explains that injured pines send chemical signals through fungal threads, prompting neighboring pines to brew bitter defensive resins in advance.
questions.retryHint: Read the last three sentences of Paragraph 4 to trace what happens after an injured pine sends chemical signals into its root tips.

questions.prompt: In Paragraph 3, the author claims that the nutrient trade between trees is not merely a one-way gift from older trees to young trees. Which evidence from Paragraph 3 best supports this claim?

options.text: Thick branches high in the canopy block sunlight from reaching small saplings on the ground.
options.diagnosticNote: Explains why young seedlings need help in summer, but does not show a two-way exchange.
options.childFeedback: Branches blocking sunlight explains why young seedlings need help in summer, not how young trees give back to older trees.

options.text: Scientists sometimes refer to older hub trees in the forest as mother trees.
options.diagnosticNote: Repeats a true detail from Paragraph 3 that does not prove that nutrients flow in both directions.
options.childFeedback: Calling older trees 'mother trees' only highlights how older trees care for young ones, without proving that young trees send nutrients back.

options.text: Young saplings always produce more carbon than towering hub trees during every season of the year.
options.diagnosticNote: Uses extreme words ('always', 'every season') and contradicts the passage.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 3 states that shaded saplings struggle to make enough sugar in summer, so they certainly do not make more carbon than tall trees in every season.

options.text: When autumn arrived and the birch leaves fell, the young firs sent small amounts of sugar back to the bare birch roots.
options.diagnosticNote: Directly proves a two-way seasonal exchange by showing young firs returning sugar to leafless birch trees in autumn.
options.childFeedback: The last sentence of Paragraph 3 proves the trade goes both ways: once autumn arrived and the tall birch trees lost their leaves, the young firs sent sugar back to the bare birch roots.

questions.provingSentenceText: Once autumn arrived and the birch leaves fell, the young firs sent small amounts of sugar back to the bare birch roots.
questions.childTip: The last sentence of Paragraph 3 proves the trade goes both ways: once autumn arrived and the tall birch trees lost their leaves, the young firs sent sugar back to the bare birch roots.
questions.parentExplanation: Focus standard ELAGSE5RI8 (Author's Claims & Supporting Evidence). To prove that the exchange is two-way rather than one-way, the reader must select the final sentence of Paragraph 3 showing young firs sending sugar back to bare birch roots in autumn.
questions.retryHint: Check the very last sentence of Paragraph 3 to see what the young fir trees did for the birch trees when autumn arrived.

questions.prompt: PART A: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?

options.text: Underground fungal networks connect forest trees into a cooperative community that shares nutrients, supports young saplings, and spreads defense warnings.
options.diagnosticNote: Synthesizes all major sections of the text: the fungal web (Para 1-2), sapling support (Para 3), defense signals (Para 4), and forest stewardship (Para 5).
options.childFeedback: Across all five paragraphs, the central idea is that underground mycorrhizal fungal networks link forest trees together to trade nutrients, feed shaded saplings, and send pest warnings.

options.text: Bark beetles are the most destructive pests in pine forests because they chew through green needles every summer.
options.diagnosticNote: Focuses only on an example from Paragraph 4 rather than the central idea of the entire passage.
options.childFeedback: Bark beetles are only one example in Paragraph 4 showing how the root web carries warning signals, not the main idea of the whole passage.

options.text: Fungal threads cannot make their own food from sunlight because they grow beneath dark leaf litter.
options.diagnosticNote: States a single supporting fact from Paragraph 2 instead of the overarching central claim.
options.childFeedback: Why fungi cannot make food from sunlight is just one detail in Paragraph 2 explaining why fungi trade minerals for tree sugar.

options.text: Foresters have completely stopped harvesting timber from hills so that fungal threads are never disturbed.
options.diagnosticNote: Uses extreme qualifiers ('completely stopped', 'never') that distort Paragraph 5's point about keeping hub trees intact.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 5 says foresters now keep older hub trees intact to protect the fungal web when caring for woods, not that all timber harvesting has stopped completely.

questions.provingSentenceText: Far from standing alone, forest trees use this living web to share food, water, and warning signals across long distances.
questions.childTip: Across all five paragraphs, the central idea is that underground mycorrhizal fungal networks link forest trees together to trade nutrients, feed shaded saplings, and send pest warnings.
questions.parentExplanation: Part A of the EBSR pair tests Central Idea synthesis (ELAGSE5RI2). Options B and C are classic 'Tiny Detail Traps' (`TRAP_TOO_NARROW`) from single paragraphs, while Option A integrates the entire passage.
questions.retryHint: Look at the last sentence of Paragraph 1, which previews all the ways forest trees use the living underground web across the article.

questions.prompt: Which quotation from the passage best supports the correct answer to Question 5?

options.text: "Each trunk rises toward the sun as if competing against its neighbors for light and space."
options.diagnosticNote: Quotes the opening surface appearance that the author immediately disproves in the rest of Paragraph 1.
options.childFeedback: This sentence from Paragraph 1 describes how trees look from above as if they are competing alone, which is the mistaken impression the author corrects.

options.text: "Far from standing alone, forest trees use this living web to share food, water, and warning signals across long distances."
options.diagnosticNote: Directly proves the central claim in Part A by summarizing how the underground web connects trees to share resources and warnings.
options.childFeedback: This quotation from Paragraph 1 directly states the passage's central idea by summing up how forest trees use the living underground web to share food, water, and warning signals.

options.text: "Because thick branches block the sun, a small seedling on the forest floor often struggles to make enough sugar to survive."
options.diagnosticNote: Describes only the problem faced by shaded seedlings in Paragraph 3 rather than the overall function of the network.
options.childFeedback: This detail from Paragraph 3 only explains why shaded seedlings struggle in summer, leaving out mineral trading and pest warning signals.

options.text: "In the past, loggers often cleared every old tree from a hillside and left young seedlings to grow in bare soil."
options.diagnosticNote: Describes outdated logging practices in Paragraph 5 rather than supporting the central claim about the fungal network.
options.childFeedback: This sentence from Paragraph 5 describes how loggers used to clear hillsides in the past, rather than how the underground fungal network connects the forest.

questions.provingSentenceText: Far from standing alone, forest trees use this living web to share food, water, and warning signals across long distances.
questions.childTip: This quotation from Paragraph 1 directly states the passage's central idea by summing up how forest trees use the living underground web to share food, water, and warning signals.
questions.parentExplanation: Part B requires selecting the verbatim thesis statement from Paragraph 1 that encapsulates resource sharing and warning signals across the forest network.
questions.retryHint: Find the quote from Paragraph 1 that lists the three things forest trees share through the living underground web.
